sources.description:
I am an LLM researcher working on optimization and efficient training of neural networks. My current research includes low-rank pretraining, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and reducing the memory cost of language-model training.

I study how optimization and regularization affect the singular-value spectra and effective rank of weight matrices. I am interested in spectral weight decay, nuclear-norm regularization, proximal methods, and Newton-Schulz approximations. A central question is whether training can make a model easier to compress with low-rank factorization while preserving its quality. Related questions concern generalization and memorization under label noise.

Another research direction is optimization for LoRA and other low-rank parameterizations. Relevant topics include Muon-style matrix updates, optimization of factorized weights, rebalancing, spectral constraints, and convergence analysis. I want to understand both the geometry of these updates and their practical behavior when fine-tuning language models.

I also work on memory-efficient LLM pretraining. Relevant methods include low-rank gradient and optimizer-state representations, GaLore, Frugal-style methods, and low-precision optimizer states such as FP8. I am interested in their tradeoffs between model quality, training memory, throughput, and communication cost, including how those tradeoffs change with model scale.

As a secondary current interest, I am building an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness. Relevant work includes explicit context management, structured LLM decisions, application-controlled tools, and paper retrieval and relevance ranking using lexical or embedding-based methods.

I have not specified hard topic exclusions for this digest.

matches.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights
matches.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional $\ell_2$ weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with $124$M to $500$M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At $500$M and a $4\%$ distortion budget, it reaches $1.89\times$ compression and $1.18\times$ GPU inference speedup, compared with $1.14\times$ and $1.01\times$ after standard weight decay. matches.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
matches.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. matches.title: ORCA: The Annealed Spectral Conditioning Optimizer for Faster, Better LLM Training
matches.abstract_excerpt: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. matches.title: Optimizer Geometry Sets the Pace: Spectral Learning Dynamics in Matrix Factorization
matches.abstract_excerpt: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. matches.title: Train High, Ship Low: Efficient LoRA Synchronization for Distributed On-Policy Post-Training
matches.abstract_excerpt: Transmitting LoRA adapters to rollout workers can bottleneck distributed on-policy post-training over bandwidth-constrained networks. We introduce HiLo, a compressor-agnostic framework that replaces parameter transmission with compressed gradient dissemination and local optimizer replay. matches.title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
matches.abstract_excerpt: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. However, its practical effectiveness is often limited, as the resulting linear bottleneck constrains representational capacity. To overcome these limitations, we propose an enhanced factorization scheme that increases expressive power by introducing learnable non-linear projections within the compressed embedding layer. Our method is inspired by the Kolmogorov Arnold Networks (KAN) paradigm, which replaces fixed linear transformations with learnable univariate functions. matches.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
matches.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. matches.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
matches.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. inspect:2610.11730.question: For LLaMA 124M–500M, what baselines and controls establish matched validation loss, and what are the measured compression ratios, inference speedups, and training-time costs of spectral weight decay?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

We introduced spectral weight decay by replacing the squared Frobenius penalty of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay with the nuclear norm. Its decoupled post-step correction shrinks the spectrum of the updated weights additively, with a stronger relative effect on smaller singular values. The connection to approximate proximal descent supports this choice of update order. Our analysis also shows that pre- and post-step spectral updates can differ more substantially than their ℓ 2 \ell_{2} counterparts near rank deficiency. Across 124 124 M to 500 500 M LLaMA models trained with Adam-family optimizers, the resulting low-effective-rank structure improves post-training compression under matched validation-loss budgets. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, we obtain 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. The benefits extend beyond compression. Under fixed-horizon training with noisy labels, spectral regularization reduces memorization and improves clean-test accuracy on image and text classification tasks. These observations are consistent with the view that concentrating the weight spectrum limits the capacity available to fit corrupted labels. The benefits depend on when and how spectral regularization is applied. Short fine-tuning from a conventional-weight-decay checkpoint incurs a larger loss penalty for rank reduction than regularization during pretraining. Optimizer choice also matters: Adam and Lion exhibit a favorable trade-off between loss and rank, whereas the Muon runs show a steeper loss increase as rank decreases. Adapting spectral regularization to matrix-aware optimizers and reducing the cost of preparing existing checkpoints for low-rank compression remain open problems.

Cuttlefish [ Wang et al., 2023 ] is a direct training-time alternative based on a simple idea: it starts with full-rank training, waits for the stable ranks of the layers to converge, then factorizes each layer at the corresponding rank and continues training the low-rank factors. Like spectral weight decay, it modifies the model during training rather than compressing a fixed checkpoint. Across all four matched settings in Figure 12 , spectral weight decay reaches a substantially lower final effective rank at comparable validation loss. Figure 12 : Training trajectories for spectral weight decay and Cuttlefish on 124 124 M-parameter LLaMA models trained on FineWeb-Edu. Each column compares the spectral coefficient λ \lambda with the indicated Cuttlefish rank fraction r frac r_{\mathrm{frac}} .

BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

• We formulate spectral weight decay as decoupled nuclear-norm regularization, derive its additive singular-value shrinkage, and connect the update to approximate proximal descent. • Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay improves low-rank compression and inference speed over standard weight decay at matched validation loss. It also outperforms Cuttlefish and Prehab in matched compression comparisons. • On image and text classification tasks, spectral weight decay improves fixed-horizon robustness to label noise over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization.

We introduced spectral weight decay by replacing the squared Frobenius penalty of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay with the nuclear norm. Its decoupled post-step correction shrinks the spectrum of the updated weights additively, with a stronger relative effect on smaller singular values. The connection to approximate proximal descent supports this choice of update order. Our analysis also shows that pre- and post-step spectral updates can differ more substantially than their ℓ 2 \ell_{2} counterparts near rank deficiency. Across 124 124 M to 500 500 M LLaMA models trained with Adam-family optimizers, the resulting low-effective-rank structure improves post-training compression under matched validation-loss budgets. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, we obtain 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. The benefits extend beyond compression. Under fixed-horizon training with noisy labels, spectral regularization reduces memorization and improves clean-test accuracy on image and text classification tasks. These observations are consistent with the view that concentrating the weight spectrum limits the capacity available to fit corrupted labels. The benefits depend on when and how spectral regularization is applied. Short fine-tuning from a conventional-weight-decay checkpoint incurs a larger loss penalty for rank reduction than regularization during pretraining. Optimizer choice also matters: Adam and Lion exhibit a favorable trade-off between loss and rank, whereas the Muon runs show a steeper loss increase as rank decreases. Adapting spectral regularization to matrix-aware optimizers and reducing the cost of preparing existing checkpoints for low-rank compression remain open problems.

Cuttlefish [ Wang et al., 2023 ] is a direct training-time alternative based on a simple idea: it starts with full-rank training, waits for the stable ranks of the layers to converge, then factorizes each layer at the corresponding rank and continues training the low-rank factors. Like spectral weight decay, it modifies the model during training rather than compressing a fixed checkpoint. Across all four matched settings in Figure 12 , spectral weight decay reaches a substantially lower final effective rank at comparable validation loss. Figure 12 : Training trajectories for spectral weight decay and Cuttlefish on 124 124 M-parameter LLaMA models trained on FineWeb-Edu. Each column compares the spectral coefficient λ \lambda with the indicated Cuttlefish rank fraction r frac r_{\mathrm{frac}} .

passages.text: We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

passages.text: Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

We profile the optimizer state peak memory and wall-clock time during the pre-training experiments from Section 5.2 . Details on the memory profiling procedure can be found in Section E.8 . As shown in Table 9 , Ori exhibits a superior efficiency profile among standard, non-error-feedback gradient-subspace methods (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). In addition, as shown in Table 10 , O-LDAdam demonstrates competitive and comparable efficiency profile to the error-feedback baseline LDAdam under the large update frequency regime ( T = 200 T=200 ). Full table on pre-training of other model sizes can be found in Appendix F . Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. For instance, at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB). This confirms Ori’s tangible memory savings. On the other hand, compared to the error-feedback methods, O-LDAdam consistently yields the same memory footprint as LDAdam baselines. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

On the other hand, although O-LDAdam yields a slightly longer average update time than LDAdam with T = 200 T=200 due to the need to perform power iterations multiple times ( Algorithm 3 ), the additional cost is not prohibitively large. Moreover, O-LDAdam demonstrates a nontrivial speedup compared to the standard LDAdam setting with a per-step update schedule ( T = 1 T=1 ). Together with the model performance results shown in Table 2 , this demonstrates that O-LDAdam strikes a good balance between model performance and computational cost in the extremely low-rank regime. Table 11 presents the full results of memory and Wallclock time comparison of all the optimizer methods on the LLaMA model pre-training task on the C4 dataset. As shown by the table, our method Ori achieves superior memory and computation time profile almost across the broad, demonstrating its general efficiency under various settings. Table 11 : Memory and Wallclock Time Comparison of pre-training various sized LLaMa model on the C4 dataset.

inspect:2610.06116.question: Across the 130M–8B LLM pretraining experiments, how were Muon and ORCA matched for tokens, hyperparameter tuning, and compute, and what validation-loss gains and training-time overhead were measured?

passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. Qwen3 Pretraining Tasks. We compare Adam, Muon, and ORCA on Qwen3-style architecture. Within each model scale, all methods share the same common hyperparameters. The Qwen3 0.6B curves cover 50k optimizer steps (about 105B tokens), and the Qwen3 160M curves cover 25k optimizer steps (about 26B tokens). In both Qwen settings, both sets of loss curves show the same ordering: ORCA may fall temporarily behind Muon early in training, then crosses over and holds the advantage at the end of the observed interval. The validation-loss improvement of ORCA is therefore not confined to LLaMA, but also reproduces on the Qwen3 architecture. Larger Scale Fine-grained MoE Pretrining. We observed router perturbations under a fixed global release point, so we release the orthogonal constraint layerwise: at 20 % 20\% of training in the first layer and at 60 % 60\% in the last layer, with release times linearly interpolated across layers. We use top- 4 4 routing with 64 64 experts in the MoE 0.8 0.8 B model ( 0.24 0.24 B active parameters) and 64 64 experts in the MoE 8 8 B model ( 1 1 B active parameters) ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . Due to computational budget constraints, we focus our comparison on Muon and ORCA. ORCA achieves the lowest final loss at both 25 25 B and 50 50 B tokens for the 0.8 0.8 B model, showing that its gain persists as the token budget increases. The 8 8 B experiment extends this result to a larger model trained on 100 100 B tokens, where ORCA also finishes below Muon ( Figure 4.4 ). Across these MoE experiments, ORCA reduces final validation loss by 0.020 0.020 – 0.025 0.025 relative to Muon.

Early orthogonal shaping also benefits other base optimizers. We apply the same soft orthogonal shaping step ( 3.3 ) to Adam and SOAP on LLaMA 130M ( Vyas et al., 2025 ) . Shaping is active only during the first 25 % 25\% of training; the base optimizer then continues alone. For both optimizers, shaping temporarily raises validation loss while active, but the shaped runs overtake their baselines after its removal and finish lower. At 50k steps, it reduces Adam’s loss from 2.8824 2.8824 to 2.8435 2.8435 and SOAP’s from 2.8640 2.8640 to 2.8271 2.8271 , gains of 0.0389 0.0389 and 0.0369 0.0369 , respectively. Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. inspect:2610.04249.question: What balance and alignment assumptions underlie the singular-mode results for GD, SignGD, Muon, Shampoo, and K-FAC, and what experiments, if any, test whether these predictions apply to neural-network or LLM training?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

In contrast to the Euclidean geometry of GD, non-Euclidean optimizers transform the factorization-induced geometry in qualitatively different ways. SignGD and Adam apply coordinate-wise adaptive scaling ( Bernstein et al., 2018 ; Kingma and Ba, 2014 ) ; Muon acts directly on the spectrum of matrix updates ( Jordan et al., 2024 ) while Shampoo introduces history-dependent matrix preconditioning ( Gupta et al., 2018 ) ; and K-FAC attempts to compensate for the parameterization through curvature using approximate natural gradients ( Martens and Grosse, 2015 ) . In our study, we categorize these geometries based on their updates into Euclidean (GD), coordinate-wise (SignGD and Adam), spectral (Muon and Shampoo) and curvature based (K-FAC). These methods can reach nearly identical training losses while producing weights with different spectra, representations, and performance. Recent studies have begun to identify optimizer-dependent feature and simplicity biases, including differences between Adam and GD in nonlinear models ( Cattaneo et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ; Xie and Li, 2024 ) and between spectral and Euclidean updates in deep linear networks ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) . These findings further motivate the central question we posed, and answering this requires distinguishing how quickly modes emerge from how they settle or disappear, since an optimizer can affect these phases differently. We express effective matrix dynamics through the layer updates and derive an exact mode reduction under explicit balance and alignment assumptions. The reduction separates the contribution of the factorization from the optimizer update states.

( 𝟐 ) \mathbf{(2)} Phase laws revealing how optimizer settings shape the bias of depth. We derive birth, saturation, and decay laws that distinguish normalization, accumulated history, and damping. GD and SignGD dynamics establish contrasting reference behaviors. Instantaneous Adam identifies how a positive stabilizer restores slow dynamics at small gradient magnitudes. Ideal Muon accelerates both emergence and removal of modes in finite time. For cumulative Shampoo, an exact accumulator identity quantifies the transition from initialization dominated to history dominated dynamics. For the specified K-FAC block model, an exact birth time decomposition separates an undamped contribution from a damping-weighted GD contribution. Together, these results identify when optimizer geometry preserves, modifies, or cancels the suppression of small modes induced by depth. ( 𝟑 ) \mathbf{(3)} Numerical validation of phase laws and regime transitions. Controlled experiments in deep matrix factorization and regression verify the derived phase laws. These experiments demonstrate that settings commonly associated with numerical stability can change relative spectral progress, determining which components emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . inspect:2610.04507.question: In the module-matched rank sweep under label noise, what are the experimental controls and risk results for the 7B language model and four vision backbones versus dense fine-tuning, and at what rank does LoRA lose its parameter advantage?

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

We compare LoRA ranks up to 4 ​ d 4d with dense fine-tuning of the same qkv projections in the same six blocks, under the shared learning rate; the arms share seeds, subsets and noise draws. The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. LoRA’s parameter advantage is strongest at the cheap end and runs out in the tail; rank-one LoRA dominates dense outright on three of the four vision backbones. Rank keeps shaping generalization long after it stops saving parameters.

passages.section: Appendix C Comparisons with dense fine-tuning
passages.text: Under the shared learning rate, every post-peak rank that still saves parameters trails module-matched dense fine-tuning on the three vision backbones with a cliff (Appendix C.1 ) and on a 7 7 B language model (Appendix C.3 ). Per-arm learning rates narrow this gap without closing it (Appendix C.2 ), and Appendix C.4 explains why the tail is graded against dense rather than against the pre-peak valley.

inspect:2611.06598.question: How is behavioral rate measured in LoRA fine-tuning, which adapter-compression baselines and frozen base models are compared, and what controlled results support the claims about correction spectra and noisy training data?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter’s leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results

raining task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning depends on the receiver, target behavior, and how the required corrections are represented in the learned update.

Fine-tuning changes the behavior of a pretrained model by writing an update relative to what that model already knows. How many bits are actually required to preserve this acquired behavior? Parameter count, adapter rank, and numerical precision measure storage, but need not measure the information that matters functionally. Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) provides a clean setting for studying this question: the base model remains frozen while the learned update is isolated in a separate adapter that can be compressed after training. We take a receiver-relative rate–distortion view of this process. As illustrated in Figure 1 , fine-tuning acts as an encoder, the adapter as a finite-rate message, and the frozen model as side information available when that message is decoded. We measure rate by the exact serialized size of a compressed adapter and distortion by the behavior of the resulting composed model. For a fixed retention target, the behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} is the smallest measured rate that preserves the required fraction of the held-out fine-tuning gain. This operational definition exposes a gap between numerical and behavioral compression. Lower weight reconstruction error need not preserve more learned behavior, and comparable bit budgets can have different effects depending on where compression acts. Behavioral rate also increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budget. Most importantly, the same datasets can require substantially different rates across frozen models, with their ordering changing across receivers. A correction-gradient spectrum computed from the data and receiver ranks R ⋆ R^{\star} well within a fixed receiver, but does not transfer reliably across new receivers. Compression can also reveal structure

ction-gradient spectrum computed from the data and receiver ranks R ⋆ R^{\star} well within a fixed receiver, but does not transfer reliably across new receivers. Compression can also reveal structure within a learned update. Under deliberately corrupted reasoning supervision, fine-tuning can strongly damage the frozen model, yet aggressive compression recovers much of the lost performance and can exceed the frozen baseline. On Qwen2.5-7B, for example, GSM8K accuracy falls from 77.6% to 23.7% after corrupted fine-tuning and returns to 82.9% after compression. Singular-direction analyses show that harmful and useful effects are distributed unevenly across the update, while matched-norm controls show that the recovery is not exactly equivalent to scalar rescaling. Finally, once an update has been trained, its behavioral rate closely tracks how far it can be shrunk before losing its gain. A simple codec-specific rule, R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) ≈ α 90 / γ R^{\star}(0.90)\approx\alpha_{90}/\gamma , achieves an RMSE of 0.068 bits per value on 42 checkpoints from five receivers not used to fix the rule, although the evaluation remains retrospective. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning is not an intrinsic property of the data or of parameter displacement alone: it depends on the frozen receiver, the behavior to preserve, and how the learned corrections are represented within the update.

We first test whether behavioral rate can be treated as an intrinsic property of the fine-tuning data. Figure 6 (b) measures R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) for the same three corpora across seven frozen receivers. The ordering changes with the receiver: XBRL tagging is the lowest-rate corpus for six receivers, but not for Qwen2.5-7B, where math is cheaper. Even closely related receivers can differ substantially: preserving 90% of the math gain requires 1.03 bits per value on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, compared with 0.41 on Qwen2.5-7B. Behavioral rate therefore depends on the dataset–receiver pair, rather than on the dataset alone. Section 4 motivates a receiver-relative statistic computed before training from the corrections requested by the data. We summarize the corresponding correction-gradient spectrum by its log-determinant (Appendix B.3 ). Within a fixed receiver, this quantity ranks behavioral rate well: across 24 arms and seven task families, Spearman correlation with R ⋆ ​ ( 0.90 ) R^{\star}(0.90) is ρ = 0.92 \rho=0.92 on Mistral-7B and ρ = 0.59 \rho=0.59 on Qwen2.5-7B, with a selection-adjusted permutation p = 0.0003 p=0.0003 (Figure 6 (a)). This association does not transfer reliably across receivers. After fixing the statistic, correlations on additional receiver panels are − 0.1 -0.1 on Llama-3.1-8B, − 0.4 -0.4 on Qwen3-8B, and + 0.1 +0.1 on a fresh Qwen2.5-7B panel. Corpus-only quantities and quantities obtained by scoring the corpus with the frozen model likewise fail to consistently order receivers. We therefore view correction spectra as informative within-receiver descriptors of compression difficulty, rather than as universal predictors of behavioral rate. Predicting R ⋆ R^{\star} from the data and receiver alone remains open.

Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. The released benchmark contains 30 queries in each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD. According to the dataset construction record, GPT-6 Astra in ChatGPT was used to extract and generate the shared literature-search prompts. EASY supplies more identifying detail, MEDIUM removes some detail, and HARD uses shorter, less specific descriptions. These are intended difficulty levels rather than independently calibrated labels. The tiers are not independent paper pools; in particular, MEDIUM and HARD share targets with different wording. The present comparison uses the first ten IDs of each tier: EASY N001–N010, MEDIUM C001–C010, and HARD C001–C010. Each system receives the same filled item prompt: a paper-finding instruction, the 2015–2025 publication/verified-version constraint, up-to-five distinct works with exact bibliographic fields and a short match explanation, identity verification and deduplication requirements, and the idea text. The designated target is not supplied to retrieval. Original prompts and outputs are preserved; Appendix A gives the exact shared wrappers and a three-tier example. These are retrieval prompts, distinct from the internal scoring prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini were tested through their October 2026 web Deep Research interfaces; backend model/build identifiers and subscription tiers were not recorded. Idea2Prior used its API pipeline. Preserved Expert outputs identify the configured alias openai/gemini-3.8-flash ; a compatibility-protocol alias does not independently verify the upstream served model. The released native-Gemini preset is not a newly benchmarked replacement for those historical runs.

Results use final selected runs, including authorized replacements of operationally failed attempts. They therefore measure selected-result recovery, not first-attempt reliability. EASY initially produced five target hits over ten planned queries before recovery; the final selection produced nine. We retain the historical ChatGPT EASY convention of 7/10: six observed hits plus one convention-based counted hit. No returned paper or intersection is fabricated for that credit. Counting only observed hits would make ChatGPT EASY 6/10 and aggregate recovery 12/30; our primary table preserves the earlier agreed convention explicitly. These browser outputs also carry a control limitation: new conversations were used, but the operator reported ChatGPT memory/history references enabled during earlier testing. The adopted HARD comparison uses the replacement NEW report. This historical record does not establish a newly controlled, contamination-free evaluation. Future comparisons should use isolated sessions with memory disabled and a frozen protocol.

inspect:2610.31897.question: For the large-model experiments, what baselines and matched compression budgets are used, and what are the measured model-quality, compression, memory, and inference-speed results for S-SALAAD?

passages.text: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

Scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations ( Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2013 ; Gunn & Anderson, 2015 ) . Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Kuutti et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Bodmer et al., 2026 ) , while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded ( European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016 ; Shi et al., 2016 ) . These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety ( Shin & Cui, 1995 ; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004 ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Nan et al., 2026 ) .

To address memory constraints, existing compression methods use quantization ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , pruning ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank factorization ( Hsu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection 1 1 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1 ). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. Hardware-friendly patterns, including block sparsity ( Okanovic et al., 2025 ) , N : M N\!:\!M sparsity ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and row-/column-wise sparsity ( Wen et al., 2016 ) , are therefore required to translate these memory savings into efficient edge inference. A straightforward extension of SALAAD is to impose these patterns on its learned sparse components after pretraining. However, our experiments show that this post-hoc conversion can sharply degrade model performance (see Appendix A.2 ). We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining , allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

To this end, we introduce S-SALAAD ( S tructured- S parse- A nd- L ow-Rank A daptation via AD MM), a plug-and-play framework that learns structured SLR representations during pretraining for elastic compression and efficient edge inference. Based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), it induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture or optimizer update rules. Efficient low-rank updates reduce pretraining overhead, while budget-aware refinement enables zero-shot compression of a single checkpoint to multiple parameter budgets without calibration data or further training. Among these patterns, we identify block sparsity as a practical choice for elastic deployment given current technical capabilities. With dedicated CPU and GPU kernels, the resulting models advance the perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier relative to the evaluated baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: ❖ A plug-and-play framework for structured-sparsity learning. S-SALAAD jointly learns model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components under the task loss, adapting the representation to structural constraints during pretraining. S-SALAAD induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture, and it is compatible with existing optimizers.

passages.section: F.2 Qwen Inference Under a Fixed Memory Cap
passages.text: Under a constrained GPU memory budget, S-SALAAD’s memory savings also enable larger inference batches, providing additional throughput gains. Figure 25 evaluates Qwen3-1.7B on the Quadro RTX 6000 under a fixed 3.4 GB 3.4\text{\,}\mathrm{GB} peak-memory cap, with the batch size increased for each model within this limit. At a 1B parameter budget, S-SALAAD achieves 2.48 × 2.48\times the throughput of dense inference, with perplexity increasing from 12.71 to 14.06. These results show how elastic compression allows limited GPU memory to support higher throughput while offering a choice of model quality. Figure 25: Compressed Qwen3-1.7B: speedup and perplexity under a 3.4 GB 3.4\text{\,}\mathrm{GB} peak-memory cap. We increase the batch size until the cap.

passages.section: Appendix G Block Granularity and the Pareto Frontier
passages.text: Figure 26 extends the analysis in Section 5.2 by comparing the deployment trade-offs of different block granularities and the L L -only special case across model scales and hardware. (a) Llama-350M, Quadro RTX 6000. (b) Llama-1B, Quadro RTX 6000. (c) Llama-1B, RTX 2080 Ti. (d) Llama-1B, CPU. Figure 26: Perplexity against throughput on Llama for different block granularities, including the L L -only baseline. Marker radius encodes peak GPU memory with min–max scaling or peak RAM with proportional scaling, per panel. Finer blocks better preserve quality under tight compression budgets, but their additional inference overhead limits the deployment gains. On Llama-350M, coarser blocks incur a pronounced quality penalty despite their higher throughput (Figure 26(a) ). On Llama-1B, the coarsest blocks retain competitive quality and closely track the L L -only deployment trade-offs on both GPUs (Figures 26(b) and 26(c) ). On CPU, the same granularity also provides operating points that improve on L L -only (Figure 26(d) ). Together with Figure 6 , these trends indicate that larger models tolerate coarser structure, enabling more efficient inference while preserving elastic compressibility. They also support the main-text conclusion that retaining S S can improve the perplexity–memory–latency trade-offs beyond L L -only when block granularity is matched to the model and deployment hardware. Numerical results for Figure 26 are provided in Appendix H .

passages.text: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We further evaluate RoM on LoRA-based RL finetuning using the VeRL framework ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Since the other LoRA baselines do not specify an RL training recipe, we focus on comparing RoM against Adam. We train the Qwen2.5-3B base model ( Yang et al., 2024 ) using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the training split of MATH (7.5K problems) with rank r = 16 r=16 . At each rollout step, we sample 8 responses for each of 128 prompts, yielding 1024 sequences per optimization step. We use no KL penalty and train for 400 steps. Following the setup of Liu et al. (2025) , we use the bare questions as prompts with no chat template. We evaluate the finetuned model using greedy decoding on three held-out benchmarks: MATH-500 (500 examples), GSM8K test (1319 examples), and OlympiadBench ( He et al., 2024 ) (674 examples). We tune Adam’s learning rate on a logarithmic grid and select 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} . We use the same learning rate for RoM without further tuning. Table 4: Final downstream accuracy (%) after GRPO finetuning over three independent runs. Results are mean ± \pm standard deviation. “Time” denotes the median end-to-end wall clock time per optimizer step, normalized to Adam. Figure 2 shows evaluation accuracy on the three held-out benchmarks throughout RL finetuning. RoM improves accuracy faster than Adam and reaches higher final accuracy on all three benchmarks. Table 4 reports the final evaluation results over three independent runs. Unlike in SFT, where downstream differences among optimizers are relatively small, RoM shows a clearer advantage over Adam in RL finetuning, while requiring only 1.08 × 1.08\times the per-step training time on 4 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs.

We presented RoM, a manifold-based optimizer for LoRA that directly optimizes the fixed-rank weight adaptation while avoiding the redundancy of factorized parameterizations. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, RoM enables efficient Riemannian optimization with memory requirement comparable to conventional LoRA optimization. Across supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning experiments, RoM consistently achieves lower validation loss than existing LoRA optimizers, while also improving downstream performance in the RL setting. Ablation experiments further show that both normalization and rotation contribute to its optimization performance.

passages.text: Theoretically, we show that the BMuon oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under an induced norm Ω α , K \Omega_{\alpha,K} , where α \alpha controls the strength of channel reweighting and K K is the global budget over the N N hidden channels. This family recovers Muon when α = 0 \alpha=0 or K = N K=N . At α = 1 \alpha=1 , its unit ball is the convex hull of operator-norm-bounded updates supported on at most K K coupled hidden channels. This is related to group k k -support norms through the use of structured support ( Argyriou et al., 2012 ; Rao et al., 2017 ) , but its atoms are bounded in operator norm rather than Euclidean norm. It is also related to spectral k k -support norms ( McDonald et al., 2014 ; McDonald et al., 2016 ) , but differs in the notion of sparsity: spectral k k -support uses sparsity in singular values, whereas BMuon uses MLP-channel sparsity. At α = K = 1 \alpha=K=1 , the norm reduces to an ℓ 1 \ell_{1} aggregation over coupled channel groups, yielding a group-lasso-like geometry ( Yuan and Lin, 2006 ) . We then characterize the representation cost induced by BMuon. Following Dai et al. (2021) , this is the minimum parameter-space cost among exact two-matrix factorizations that realize the same linear predictor. We prove that, under an explicit budget-scarcity condition, every minimum-cost BMuon factorization is width-minimal, whereas Muon’s minimum cost can also be attained by factorizations with redundant hidden width.

Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Under gradual pruning, using the learned allocations themselves to rank channels further improves performance, showing that they also provide a useful measure of channel importance. The non-uniform architectures identified by BMuon in the gradual-pruning experiments also outperform matched uniform-width architectures when retrained from scratch, providing evidence that the learned allocation captures useful differences in how MLP capacity should be distributed across layers. Finally, on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning, showing that the effect extends to language modeling at substantially larger scale.
