(a) Llama-350M, Quadro RTX 6000. (b) Llama-1B, Quadro RTX 6000. (c) Llama-1B, RTX 2080 Ti. (d) Llama-1B, CPU. Figure 26: Perplexity against throughput on Llama for different block granularities, including the L L -only baseline. Marker radius encodes peak GPU memory with min–max scaling or peak RAM with proportional scaling, per panel. Finer blocks better preserve quality under tight compression budgets, but their additional inference overhead limits the deployment gains. On Llama-350M, coarser blocks incur a pronounced quality penalty despite their higher throughput (Figure 26(a) ). On Llama-1B, the coarsest blocks retain competitive quality and closely track the L L -only deployment trade-offs on both GPUs (Figures 26(b) and 26(c) ). On CPU, the same granularity also provides operating points that improve on L L -only (Figure 26(d) ). Together with Figure 6 , these trends indicate that larger models tolerate coarser structure, enabling more efficient inference while preserving elastic compressibility. They also support the main-text conclusion that retaining S S can improve the perplexity–memory–latency trade-offs beyond L L -only when block granularity is matched to the model and deployment hardware. Numerical results for Figure 26 are provided in Appendix H .

passages.text: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We further evaluate RoM on LoRA-based RL finetuning using the VeRL framework ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Since the other LoRA baselines do not specify an RL training recipe, we focus on comparing RoM against Adam. We train the Qwen2.5-3B base model ( Yang et al., 2024 ) using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the training split of MATH (7.5K problems) with rank r = 16 r=16 . At each rollout step, we sample 8 responses for each of 128 prompts, yielding 1024 sequences per optimization step. We use no KL penalty and train for 400 steps. Following the setup of Liu et al. (2025) , we use the bare questions as prompts with no chat template. We evaluate the finetuned model using greedy decoding on three held-out benchmarks: MATH-500 (500 examples), GSM8K test (1319 examples), and OlympiadBench ( He et al., 2024 ) (674 examples). We tune Adam’s learning rate on a logarithmic grid and select 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} . We use the same learning rate for RoM without further tuning. Table 4: Final downstream accuracy (%) after GRPO finetuning over three independent runs. Results are mean ± \pm standard deviation. “Time” denotes the median end-to-end wall clock time per optimizer step, normalized to Adam. Figure 2 shows evaluation accuracy on the three held-out benchmarks throughout RL finetuning. RoM improves accuracy faster than Adam and reaches higher final accuracy on all three benchmarks. Table 4 reports the final evaluation results over three independent runs. Unlike in SFT, where downstream differences among optimizers are relatively small, RoM shows a clearer advantage over Adam in RL finetuning, while requiring only 1.08 × 1.08\times the per-step training time on 4 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs.

We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

Large language models (LLMs) based on the transformer architecture ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) have achieved remarkable success in recent years ( Brown et al., 2020 ; Touvron et al., 2023 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . These models typically adopt a pretraining-finetuning paradigm, where large-scale pretraining equips a model with general capabilities and subsequent finetuning adapts it to specific downstream applications. However, as LLMs grow to billions of parameters, full-parameter finetuning becomes expensive in both computation and memory. Such a challenge has motivated the development of parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , which only update a small fraction of all parameters. Among these approaches, low-rank adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2022 ) has emerged as a particularly effective method and has been widely adopted. LoRA freezes the pretrained weights and parametrizes the weight updates as products of low-rank matrices, substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters and the memory footprint, while maintaining competitive performance. Compared with full-parameter training, LoRA exhibits a unique geometric structure induced by its low-rank factorization. Specifically, the low-rank matrices have infinitely many reparameterizations that represent the same weight update, since the model’s output depends on these low-rank factors only through their product. This invariance, commonly referred to as gauge symmetry, suggests that optimization should respect the underlying geometry of the weight space of the LoRA parametrization. Motivated by this observation, we revisit the optimization of LoRA and aim to explicitly incorporate its gauge symmetry into the design of the optimization algorithm.

We design our optimizer on the manifold of fixed-rank matrices, aiming to optimize the product of the low-rank factors directly rather than each factor separately. We extend the recent advances in matrix optimizers ( Gong et al., 2026 ; Jordan et al., 2024 ; Vyas et al., 2025 ) to the fixed-rank manifold by interpreting their update rules as normalization under a rotated basis. Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold. By exploiting the low-rank structure of tangent vectors, all operations can be performed using thin factors without materializing full weight-sized matrices. We refer to our proposed optimizer as RoM ( Ro tated M anifold Optimization). We evaluate RoM on supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks. RoM achieves substantially lower held-out loss and better or comparable downstream task performance compared with other LoRA optimizers, with only modest additional computational overhead.

We further evaluate RoM on LoRA-based RL finetuning using the VeRL framework ( Sheng et al., 2025 ) . Since the other LoRA baselines do not specify an RL training recipe, we focus on comparing RoM against Adam. We train the Qwen2.5-3B base model ( Yang et al., 2024 ) using GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the training split of MATH (7.5K problems) with rank r = 16 r=16 . At each rollout step, we sample 8 responses for each of 128 prompts, yielding 1024 sequences per optimization step. We use no KL penalty and train for 400 steps. Following the setup of Liu et al. (2025) , we use the bare questions as prompts with no chat template. We evaluate the finetuned model using greedy decoding on three held-out benchmarks: MATH-500 (500 examples), GSM8K test (1319 examples), and OlympiadBench ( He et al., 2024 ) (674 examples). We tune Adam’s learning rate on a logarithmic grid and select 3 × 10 − 6 3\times 10^{-6} . We use the same learning rate for RoM without further tuning. Solving the exact allocation problem at every training step is expensive. We therefore derive a minorization–maximization surrogate that yields a tractable allocation update, followed by the corresponding weighted Muon update. On CIFAR-100 and ImageNet-1K, BMuon outperforms Muon under both gradual and post-training global MLP-channel pruning, even when both use the same magnitude-based pruning criterion. Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply under post-training MLP-channel pruning, motivating the question of whether Muon’s spectral geometry can be modified to favor structured compressibility. BMuon addresses this question by reweighting hidden channels within Muon’s spectral-norm constraints and making them compete for a global budget. We show that the resulting norm family recovers Muon and connects it to channel-sparse geometries. In linear two-factor models, Muon admits minimum-cost factorizations with redundant hidden width, whereas under a sufficiently scarce BMuon budget every minimum-cost factorization is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a tractable minorization–maximization approximation to the global allocation oracle. Across vision and language models, BMuon is substantially more robust than Muon to magnitude-based MLP-channel pruning. The learned allocation also provides an effective pruning score and identifies useful non-uniform MLP architectures when retrained from scratch. Several questions remain open. Our theoretical results characterize representation cost in linear two-factor models; studying the implicit bias of BMuon training, particularly beyond the linear setting, is an important direction for future work. Another direction is to design a practical BMuon algorithm with provable approximation guarantees to the oracle. Our experiments focus on MLP hidden channels, and extending the global budget to other structured components of Transformers remains to be explored. Finally, BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments; characterizing this tradeoff at larger model scales is a natural direction for future work.

2610.10965:ee0761f47a5fec96b92ec48431d20.question: In NanoGPT experiments, how does Spectrally Targeted Muon compare with full Muon and normalized SGD on validation loss, effective rank of weights and updates, and training step time or compute overhead under matched training budgets?

passages.text: The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Intuitively, an update that keeps pushing along the leading singular directions of a matrix reinforces what is already there, while a full-spectrum update mostly rotates the basis and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Figure 5 (c) plots these against the final loss. Figure 5 (a) shows the same thing with the isospectral tangent metric of Section 3.3 . Every optimizer puts more of its update into the parameter’s own basis than a random update would, and tangent alignment rises for every optimizer over training, fastest during the cooldown. Among the targeted variants of Muon, the bottom targeted versions show higher alignment than Muon, while the top targeted versions show lower alignment. This is reversed compared to the CIFAR experiments, but it reveals the same underlying phenomenon. In the NanoGPT domain, the targeted region has its magnitude raised, while the remaining regions are relatively suppressed. Therefore, it is simply the top few directions of the gradient which lie within the existing basis of the parameter, and the more you shrink them in the update, the less poorly conditioned the parameter matrices become. Note that structure and performance don’t move together: AdamW collapses rank and still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. Our work also suggests an explanation as to why warmup costs Muon but helps AdamW, using the structural plots. AdamW is slow to build structure: its zero-initialized output projections take the whole run to build rank and are still rising at the end (Figure 4 (d)), its early updates lie almost entirely in the parameters’ own frame (Figure 5 (a)), and its gradients have the lowest effective rank of any optimizer over the first hundred steps, lower than any Muon variant that builds structure at all. An elementwise normalized update builds a matrix one bounded increment at a time, so how well it builds depends on how big the first steps are, and with warmup AdamW ends with higher parameter rank and lower loss. An orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step, so Muon’s structure is the same with or without warmup and warmup only throws away full-rate steps.

In this paper, we developed a spectrally targeted variant of the Muon optimizer in order to explore why Muon has so much experimental success. By targeting Muon to act on certain singular values either above or below a certain threshold τ , \tau, we were able to do more specific experiments on Muon’s behavior. From our experiments on CIFAR-10, we concluded that Muon’s accuracy improvement requires normalization of all the singular values; by varying τ , \tau, we found that if we normalize singular values, we will measure better evaluation accuracies. However, normalizing only the top singular values yields better tangent alignment and stable weight spectra, hence the primary structural improvements of Muon result from normalizing large singular values, although normalizing smaller ones is important as well.

From our experiments on NanoGPT, we concluded that the small singular values of the momentum are not noise but directions the model can feasibly train on once they are amplified. Orthogonalizing everything but the few largest singular values nearly matches Muon, while orthogonalizing only the top buys an early lead over AdamW and then falls behind even normalized SGD. Keeping the top from dominating the update is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; the tangent alignment shows that the top singular directions are the ones that lie outside the tangent space of the isospectral manifold, so they are what changes the spectrum. This is cheap, however, and is not what drives the loss, as AdamW collapses rank and still performs well. AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, because an elementwise normalized update must build a matrix out of many low rank steps, where an orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step. This explains AdamW’s slower start and why warmup helps it but hurts Muon. Finally, the effective rank of the gradient becomes an effective tool to determine position in the loss landscape, and also shows the difference between optimizers in where the early steps take the parameters.

In future work, we could study the effect on larger transformers to see if our observations scale. Also, since matrices spectra sit at different scale, a threshold relative to the bulk of each spectrum would remove the impact of orthogonalizing a different fraction of directions for each matrix. The radial component of the update also defines an equilibrium weight decay that varies over training and across optimizers, which could be used to create some form of preconditioned weight decay which would prevent change in the spectrum. Given our results, it would also be interesting to consider whether dynamically adapting τ \tau might improve results, as we could normalize either small or large singular values depending on how far along we are in our training.

What are the matched retrievers, token budgets, latency costs, and stated limitations?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.
Table 1 compares answer accuracy, evidence recall, and search resource use across the three benchmarks.

CORE achieves the highest answer accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark group, producing new state-of-the-art results. On BrowseComp-Plus, it improves both metrics over the stronger baseline, OpenResearcher, for all three agent models. The gains are largest for Qwen3.8-27B, at 6.39 points in accuracy and 7.40 points in recall. On BrowseComp-Wikipedia, CORE keeps its lead across all three agents. With GPT-5.4, it improves both metrics by more than eight points over OpenResearcher. Higher accuracy therefore comes with broader coverage of the annotated relevant documents in both the web and Wikipedia corpora. See some case studies in Appendix C .

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Trace-norm regularization then selects a low-rank representative among all matrices that induce the same observed output. This yields exact low-rank existence results without linearizing the network around the pretrained weights. draft.reason: Ten inspected papers cover the user's main research directions, including training for compressibility, spectral optimization, LoRA, memory-efficient pretraining, and paper retrieval. Unresolved uncertainties that could change the selection include end-to-end training-memory and compute costs for several methods, and whether results beyond the tested models and tasks generalize.

selections.summary: Spectral weight decay applies a post-step nuclear-norm correction. On 124M–500M LLaMA models, the authors report lower effective rank and better SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss; at 500M and a 4% distortion budget, they report 1.89× compression and 1.18× GPU inference speedup, versus 1.14× and 1.01× with standard weight decay.
selections.relevance: Directly addresses whether regularization during training can improve low-rank compressibility without sacrificing validation loss, as well as memorization under label noise.

evidence.quote: Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss.

At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay.

selections.summary: Ori tracks drifting gradient subspaces with streaming k-PCA. In a 1B LLaMA pretraining comparison at rank 32, the reported optimizer-step peak-memory increment is 0.2487 GB versus 0.3385 GB for GaLore; the reported average update times are 12.6705 and 13.0401 seconds per step, respectively.
selections.relevance: A direct test of the quality–memory–time tradeoff for low-rank LLM pretraining. The memory figure is an optimizer-step increment, not total peak training memory.

evidence.quote: At rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB).
Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step.

selections.summary: ORCA applies soft orthogonality regularization early in LLM training and then removes it. The authors report final validation-loss reductions of 0.02–0.04 versus Muon in most experiments, across architectures up to an 8B MoE model.
selections.relevance: Tests how temporary spectral shaping affects LLM optimization and quality, with an important contrast to persistent low-rank-inducing regularization.

evidence.quote: In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam.
During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty
Then directly removes it at a single switch point.

selections.summary: Derives singular-mode birth, saturation, and decay laws for several optimizer geometries in deep matrix factorization. Controlled matrix-factorization and regression experiments test the phase laws.
selections.relevance: Provides a theoretical framework for how Muon, Adam-like updates, Shampoo, and curvature correction may alter low-rank bias; its direct empirical scope is narrower than LLM training.

evidence.quote: Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC.
Controlled experiments in deep matrix factorization and regression verify the derived phase laws.

selections.summary: A module-matched LoRA rank sweep under label noise compares adapters with dense fine-tuning of the same modules. The authors find a second descent, but no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense risk; the 7B language-model experiment likewise remains short of dense at every measured rank.
selections.relevance: Directly connects LoRA rank, parameter efficiency, generalization, and memorization under noisy labels.

selections.summary: Defines behavioral rate as the serialized adapter size needed to retain a specified fraction of held-out fine-tuning gain. The measured rate varies with the frozen base model; correction-spectrum associations rank rates within some receivers but do not transfer reliably to others.
selections.relevance: Offers a behavioral rather than purely numerical measure of LoRA compressibility, including experiments with corrupted fine-tuning data.

evidence.quote: We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain.
This association does not transfer reliably across receivers.

selections.summary: Idea2Prior combines identity verification, abstract assessment, citation expansion, and bounded evidence-based ranking for idea-to-paper retrieval. In a historical 30-query comparison, its reported Hit@5 is 16/30; the evaluation has overlapping targets and a convention-based credit in one baseline.
selections.relevance: Directly informs the user's research-digest agent design, especially auditable candidate selection and the need to distinguish retrieval failures from ranking failures.

evidence.quote: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking.
The small, overlapping target set and historical protocol do not support a broad or statistically established superiority claim.

selections.summary: RoM optimizes LoRA updates on a fixed-rank manifold while accounting for factorization symmetry. In rank-16 Qwen2.5-3B RL fine-tuning, the authors report higher accuracy than Adam on three held-out benchmarks with 1.08× per-step time.
selections.relevance: A practical geometry-aware approach to optimizing low-rank adapters, with measured performance and time tradeoffs.

evidence.quote: Our optimizer applies row and column normalization in a conditioning frame defined by the left singular vectors of the tangent momentum, projects the resulting direction back onto the tangent space, and retracts to the fixed-rank manifold.
RoM improves accuracy faster than Adam and reaches higher final accuracy on all three benchmarks.
while requiring only 1.08 × 1.08\times the per-step training time on 4 NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPUs.

selections.summary: BMuon changes Muon's geometry to allocate a global budget across MLP channels. The authors report greater robustness to post-training channel pruning in vision models and a 1B LLaMA-style model, while noting a possible dense-quality tradeoff in language modeling.
selections.relevance: Connects optimizer geometry to training-time structured compressibility, although channel pruning differs from low-rank factorization.

evidence.quote: on a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves robustness to post-training global MLP-channel pruning
BMuon can trade dense-model quality for greater pruning robustness, as observed in our language-model experiments

selections.summary: S-SALAAD jointly learns model weights and structured sparse-plus-low-rank components for elastic compression. For Qwen3-1.7B under a 3.4 GB inference-memory cap, the authors report 2.48× dense throughput at a 1B-parameter budget, with perplexity rising from 12.71 to 14.06.
selections.relevance: Tests whether learning compressible structure during training translates into an actual memory–throughput benefit, while exposing a quality cost.

evidence.quote: jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training.
At a 1B parameter budget, S-SALAAD achieves 2.48 × 2.48\times the throughput of dense inference, with perplexity increasing from 12.71 to 14.06.

limitations: These are author-reported findings from supplied abstracts and retrieved HTML passages, not independently reproduced results.
Several retrieved passages do not establish total peak training memory, full compute overhead, or robustness beyond the tested models and tasks.
No code repositories were independently checked; a linked implementation alone would not establish reproducibility.

profile.summary: LLM research focused on optimization, low-rank and memory-efficient training, spectral regularization, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, and an AI research-digest agent.

topics.name: Generalization and memorization under label noise
Optimization for LoRA and low-rank parameterizations
AI research digest agents and paper retrieval

goals: Understand how optimization and regularization affect singular-value spectra and the effective rank of weight matrices.
Determine whether training can improve low-rank compressibility while preserving model quality.
Understand the geometry and practical language-model fine-tuning behavior of LoRA and other low-rank updates.
Evaluate tradeoffs among model quality, memory, throughput, and communication cost across model scales.
Build an AI research digest agent with a handwritten harness.

proposed.relevance: Directly addresses whether regularization during training can improve low-rank compressibility without sacrificing validation loss, as well as memorization under label noise.
A direct test of the quality–memory–time tradeoff for low-rank LLM pretraining. The memory figure is an optimizer-step increment, not total peak training memory.
Tests how temporary spectral shaping affects LLM optimization and quality, with an important contrast to persistent low-rank-inducing regularization.
Provides a theoretical framework for how Muon, Adam-like updates, Shampoo, and curvature correction may alter low-rank bias; its direct empirical scope is narrower than LLM training.
Directly connects LoRA rank, parameter efficiency, generalization, and memorization under noisy labels.
Offers a behavioral rather than purely numerical measure of LoRA compressibility, including experiments with corrupted fine-tuning data.
Directly informs the user's research-digest agent design, especially auditable candidate selection and the need to distinguish retrieval failures from ranking failures.
A practical geometry-aware approach to optimizing low-rank adapters, with measured performance and time tradeoffs.
Connects optimizer geometry to training-time structured compressibility, although channel pruning differs from low-rank factorization.
Tests whether learning compressible structure during training translates into an actual memory–throughput benefit, while exposing a quality cost.

candidates.title: The Behavioral Rate of Fine-Tuning: Compression as a Measure of Useful Information
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate $R^\star$ as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: Rotated Manifold Optimization for Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.
candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: BMuon: Budgeting Muon's Spectral Geometry for Structured Compressibility
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. candidates.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. candidates.title: Optimizer Geometry Sets the Pace: Spectral Learning Dynamics in Matrix Factorization
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. candidates.title: LoRA's Second Descent Extends Beyond Parameter Parity
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter's rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. candidates.title: Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional $\ell_2$ weight decay near rank deficiency. candidates.title: ORCA: The Annealed Spectral Conditioning Optimizer for Faster, Better LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early
candidates.label: relevant

candidates.title: Learning Structured Sparsity for Large Models: Bridging Model Compressibility and Efficient Inference
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. candidates.title: Idea2Prior: Auditable Paper Retrieval and Ranking from Research Ideas
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present IDEA2PRIOR, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. candidates.title: How Finite-Rank Bottlenecks Shape the Low-Rank Adaptation Landscape
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. candidates.title: A Riemannian Geometry for Low-rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix $BA^\top$. candidates.title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. candidates.title: Rethinking LoRA Initialization for Robust Asymmetric Learning Rates
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix optimizers have emerged as a promising direction, with Muon standing out as a prominent design. Revisiting Muon through its full-Gram representation, we observe that it jointly processes marginal-scale and interaction information. This opens an alternative way to organize geometric information hierarchically, motivating the Normalize-Then-Precondition framework. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. candidates.title: Scaling Repeated-Data Pretraining: Batch Size, Regularization, and GPU-Time Tradeoffs
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We study pretraining when compute is abundant but unique training data are finite, requiring repeated training on the same data. We first revisit infinite-compute pretraining (Kim et al. 2026) and show that its frontier depends critically on choices previously fixed or studied only in isolation. candidates.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. candidates.abstract_excerpt: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Analog in-memory computing is a promising platform for on-device execution of large language models because it performs matrix--vector multiplications (MVMs) in memory and in parallel, reducing data movement. However, limited digital-to-analog converter precision, input noise, and finite conductance states can degrade model accuracy, while full-model retraining to address these effects can be costly. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become a standard approach for parameter-efficient fine-tuning, yet a fundamental practical question remains unresolved: how should the adapter rank be chosen? An overly small rank may lead to a poorly conditioned optimization landscape, whereas an unnecessarily large rank sacrifices the efficiency that motivates LoRA in the first place. candidates.title: FedLore: Communication and Memory Efficient Federated Learning via Shared Gradient Low-Rank Projection
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Federated training of foundation models is constrained by client memory and communication costs. LoRA-based methods reduce these costs through low-rank adapters, but their fixed rank budget can limit adaptation. Gradient low-rank optimization offers greater flexibility, yet independently chosen client subspaces create a problem we term \emph{subspace fragmentation}: local projections interact with data heterogeneity to bias aggregated directions, while aggregation can increase update rank and communication cost. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) provides a parameter-efficient approach to continual learning, but its nominal rank can conceal a loss of effective adaptation capacity. We identify \emph{spectral plasticity collapse}: during sequential adaptation, update energy becomes concentrated in a small subset of singular modes, leaving much of the available low-rank space underutilized. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. We introduce LoGRA, an approach to RL post-training that reduces memory by retaining useful learning signals in low-rank gradient sketches. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Power-law learning curves are often treated as fixed properties of a model and its data, although learning-rate and batch-size schedules can change the observed loss. We study this dependence in noisy online SGD with linear random features. Conditional on the representation, an exact Volterra equation separates two response components: a forcing term that propagates unresolved target error and a memory kernel that propagates stochastic-error injections. candidates.title: DT-LoRA: Reaching Beyond the Tangent Space of Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. candidates.title: Low-rank Low Precision Training of Gaussian Processes
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Training Gaussian processes (GPs) at large scale is computationally challenging because evaluating the log-marginal likelihood and its gradients involves large, dense kernel matrices. We develop a scalable low-rank GP training approach that combines AnchorNet landmark selection with a fully independent training conditional (FITC) correction. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is the de facto method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks, achieving strong task adaptation with minimal trainable parameters and low optimization cost. Beyond this efficiency, practitioners have observed two striking properties: \textit{robustness to catastrophic forgetting} and the ability to \textit{merge independently trained adapters} into a single model that performs competitively across multiple tasks. In this work, we study how gradient noise geometry shapes Muon's preconditioning benefits. We first show, theoretically and empirically, that under the classical isotropic noise assumption, Muon offers no acceleration beyond a rescaling of the learning rate. candidates.title: DictLLM: Post-training Compression of Large Language Model with Dictionary Kernels
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices requires balancing performance with compute and memory constraints. Post-training compression is an effective approach to managing this trade-off, while requiring much less computation than in-training counterparts. We propose DictLLM, a dictionary-based compression scheme in which weight matrices within grouped layers are decomposed into a shared dictionary and layer-specific sparse coefficients, directly obtained from a pre-trained model without further training. candidates.title: Spectrally Targeted Muon
candidates.abstract_excerpt: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. Recent studies of gradient flow under small initialization have analyzed how trajectories escape from a neighborhood of the origin and approach their first nonzero stationary point. In this paper, we study continuous-time dynamics that applies a finite number of Newton-Schulz iterations to the normalized matrix gradient (Muon). candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning by learning low-rank weight updates. Increasing rank expands adaptation capacity, but does not guarantee that all learned directions improve downstream performance. In a diagnostic experiment with rank-16 LoRA, we show that retaining only the top singular components achieves the best performance, whereas adding further components degrades it. Lowering the training rank may limit the capacity a workload needs, while adaptive optimizer updates are difficult to compress. candidates.title: A KAN-based Non-linear Factorization for Embedding Layer Compression
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Among existing embedding compression approaches, low-rank factorization provides a simple and mathematically principled solution by approximating the embedding matrix with a reduced-rank decomposition. However, its practical effectiveness is often limited, as the resulting linear bottleneck constrains representational capacity. candidates.title: SciCurateBench: Curating Experimental Data from Heterogeneous Scientific Literature with Verbal-Action Agents
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Scientific research increasingly depends on curating experimental data from literature. Scientific data curation requires verifying exact experimental conditions (e.g., specific assays, clinical outcomes, and data availability) across long, heterogeneous files, which is a highly time-consuming process. Existing benchmarks evaluate only broad relevance on short queries, failing to capture this complexity. candidates.title: MemCredit: From Relevance to Utility for Decision-Time Memory in Long-Horizon Web Agents
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly operate over long Web interaction histories, making memory management critical for reliable and efficient decision making. Existing methods primarily optimize storage, retrieval, or compression, but the memories most semantically relevant to the current state are not necessarily those that most improve the agent's action. candidates.title: CORE: Coarse-to-Fine Search with Context Management for Deep Research
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent's context for the rest of the trajectory. candidates.title: ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research
candidates.abstract_excerpt: What makes great scientists great? Even as AI systems start to make progress on open problems, scientists remain far ahead of them at sensing which prior idea, buried in an ever-growing archive of research, a new problem needs. To study this skill, we draw on researchers who know firsthand which earlier work advanced their completed projects, with papers serving as pointers to the ideas within. candidates.title: Agent-Controlled Forgetting for Tool-Using Agents: Reversible Context Curation in Practice
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Tool-using agents repeatedly carry observations whose useful content can be much smaller than their original payload. We study agent-controlled forgetting: the acting model selects previously observed tool results, replaces each with a short note at its original position, and retains the exact original in a recoverable archive. A Python harness exposes batch archival and explicit recovery without task-specific model training, while protecting user instructions and assistant messages from these operations.
